I chose to retool Plant 6 rather than sell or close it.

Retooling costs $30.0 million once, which the Company's $444.9 million of liquidity covers easily. It lifts operating income by $7.5 million a year, a payback of roughly four years, and the plant turns from a loss of $9.0 million to a loss of $1.5 million after corporate costs, with a path toward profit as volume is spread over automated lines. Its 162 positions stay in the community, and the plant keeps its product family under the Company's control, with its quality and customer relationships intact.

Selling would give $37.5 million once but cut operating income by $15.3 million a year, because $24.3 million of corporate cost stays behind. The buyer's commitment to 171 jobs lasts only two years, after which the employees' future depends on a buyer's choices, and we would lose the community's manufacturing base without control over it.

Closing gives the largest gain, $16.5 million a year, but it removes all 190 local jobs and the Great Plains site. The other plants could absorb the work, but the cost falls on the workers and community, and the saving depends on moving work over a long distance with a $10.0 million one-time charge and a loss of the plant's skilled workforce.

Under retooling, the 28 employees not needed on the automated line are offered positions at the other plants, which need workers and hire about 500 people a year. Management expects about 15% of those offered to accept, so relocation help of $20,000 a person and the offer itself should give most of them a path to work without severance. No one is eliminated. Retooling is the choice that best serves employees, the community and shareholders together over twenty years.

I chose to retool Plant 6. Of the three options, retooling is the only one that keeps jobs at the plant on a lasting basis. Closing would end 190 local positions and cost $10.0 million up front, and the relocated jobs would be far from the community and at most 15% of those offered would accept. Selling keeps 171 jobs, but only for at least two years, and it cuts the Company's operating income by $15.3 million a year, so the workforce's protection would lapse while the plant's value leaves the Company.

Retooling costs $30.0 million once, which is within available liquidity of $444.9 million, and it raises operating income by $7.5 million a year. The plant's operating result improves to -$1.5 million after corporate costs, and the retooled plant keeps 162 of its 190 positions. Its local payroll falls to $8.9 million from $10.5 million, a reduction that the automation accounts for, not a cut in wages.

For the 28 people not needed at the plant, I will offer positions at the other plants first. The plants hire about 500 people a year from outside, so these roles can be filled from within. Relocation help of $20,000 per person is available, and anyone who declines the offer would be a severance case. Those who take the move keep their jobs and their pay, and the Company avoids the cost of hiring from outside.

Over twenty years, this option preserves the largest share of local employment, keeps the community's supplier and environmental relationships in place, improves the Company's income, and gives the customers a plant that continues to build and service the machines they depend on. It is the choice that best balances the interests of all stakeholders.

I recommend retooling Plant 6. The plant is the Company's smallest and lowest-volume site, and its operating result of -$9.0 million after corporate costs is a structural problem of spreading fixed costs over too few units. Retooling, with automated welding and material handling like the larger plants, costs $30.0 million once and lifts the plant's operating result by $7.5 million a year to -$1.5 million after corporate costs. That is a permanent gain to operating income, funded comfortably from $444.9 million of available liquidity.

I compared the three options against the board's stakeholder objective over twenty years. Closing removes the plant's roughly 190 local jobs and adds $10.0 million of closure cost plus severance; it gives the largest operating-income gain on paper, but it shifts the production burden to other regions and sacrifices a community's employment base. Selling gives up $15.3 million a year of operating income, keeps 171 jobs only for at least two years, and leaves the workforce's future to a buyer. Retooling is the only option that keeps most of the workforce in place for the long term while still improving results.

Allocation: 162 employees stay at the plant, the number the retooled plant requires. The remaining 28 are offered positions at the other plants, within the expected acceptance of up to 29, with relocation support, which avoids severance and keeps those workers in the Company. Retooling also supports customers and suppliers through a more competitive plant and environmental stakeholders through the same automation of material handling. I will monitor the retooled plant's margin against the $7.5 million improvement target and report progress to the board.
